en: The Sūtra on the Dharma for Kings Spoken by the Buddha to the Devaputra Prasenajit, translated by the Da Tang Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda by imperial decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying in the city of Śrāvastī at the Jetavana Grove.
At the Jetavana Grove, he was accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus numbering one hundred thousand, all of whom were great arhats whose outflows were exhausted.
He was also accompanied by immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, great dragons among men, who were in their last birth before attaining buddhahood.

At that time, the World-Honored One was sitting cross-legged upon a sublime seat beneath a tree. In the midst of the great assembly, he universally expounded for humans and devas the subtle Dharma of his own realization—namely, that which is good in the beginning, middle, and end; skillful in its words and meaning; and the pure, singular, perfect, and stainless character of brahmacarya.

At that time, the King of Kośala, the Devaputra Prasenajit, prepared his carriage and retinue and departed from Śrāvastī for the Jeta Grove, desiring to pay homage to the World-Honored One, to offer respectful worship, and to serve and attend upon him.

Having arrived at the grove, he alighted from his carriage, adjusted his robes, and approached the Great Master’s dwelling. From afar, he saw the Tathāgata sitting beneath a tree preaching the Dharma to the assembly.

His countenance was upright and handsome; his faculties were fully subdued; his mind was serene and abided in supreme concentration. He was a dragon-elephant among men, like a lion king, like a bull king, and like a well-trained horse. He was the most supreme among humans, like a white lotus, like a tranquil pool, and like Mount Sumeru resting securely upon the great ocean. He was endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; his form and color were pervasive like a magnificent golden pillar, and he shone brilliantly like the thousand rays of the midday sun or like the full moon orb surrounded by the host of stars.
At that time, having seen this, the king was filled with great joy; his hair stood on end, and he experienced what he had never known before.

Although a consecrated Great King possesses five magnificent regalia—namely, the wish-fulfilling crest-jewel, the white parasol, the white fly-whisk, the jeweled sandals, and the jeweled sword—he cast them all aside. Donning the garments of an ordinary man and accompanied by his ministers, he proceeded with composure and right mindfulness, his senses stilled. Baring his right shoulder and adjusting his robes, he bowed low with palms joined and approached the World-Honored One. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, scattered exquisite flowers, and burned various famous incenses.
Having made these offerings, he circumambulated [the Buddha] three times to the right and withdrew to sit at one side.
Then King Prasenajit rose from his seat, and with his usual dignified demeanor, joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke thus:
"I pray only that the Great Master..."

You have enlightened me and skillfully instructed me in the Dharma for the sake of the state’s ruler, so that I may constantly enjoy peace and happiness in the present life, be reborn in the heavens after death, and maintain the continuity of a virtuous mind until the attainment of Bodhi.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Listen with a single-minded focus; this is most rare!
Who is able to pose such questions and seek the supreme provisions for enlightenment? You should practice in accordance with the Dharma and eliminate all unwholesome deeds. Why is this so?
"Great King!

If a king or a minister abandons wholesome dharmas and practices unwholesome dharmas, they will be despised by others in this present life; no one will dare to associate with them, and all will harbor doubts. They will constantly see evil dreams and have many enemies, and later they will feel remorse. After their lives end, they will fall into hell."
"Great King!

If a king or a minister distances himself from unwholesome dharmas and cultivates wholesome dharmas, he will be admired by people in this present life; all will come to him with affection and never harbor doubt. He will constantly see auspicious dreams, be able to eliminate his enemies, and have no further cause for regret. After the end of his life, he will attain rebirth in the heavens, and eventually realize the true, eternal bliss of Bodhi."

"Great King! It is, for example, like parents who cherish and love their children; they constantly wish for their peace and security, ensuring they suffer no harm or affliction, restraining them from evil conduct, and encouraging them to cultivate wholesome deeds."
"Great King!

It is the same for one who is a Son of Heaven: toward his ministers and assistants, and even down to the commoners and servants of the state, he nurtures them with kindness through the four means of integration—generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation."
At that time, having extensively performed such great benefits within his realm, that king of men accomplished two kinds of beneficial matters. What are these two?
"The King is like a parent, loving and mindful without partiality;
the people of the land are like children, all harboring loyalty and filial piety.
Furthermore, Great King!"
One who acts as a Son of Heaven should harbor benevolence and forgiveness in his heart, levy light taxes, and reduce corvée labor;
he should establish offices and assign duties without seeking excessive proliferation;
he should dismiss and punish the wicked, and reward and promote the worthy and good.
Those who are disloyal and unvirtuous should be swiftly distanced;
follow the ancient sage-kings and do not carry out executions. Why is this?
Those born into the human realm are moved by superior conditions; if one were to take their life, they would certainly incur an evil retribution.
Great King!
You should always single-mindedly revere the Triple Gem and never give rise to false views.
After my parinirvāṇa, the Dharma shall be entrusted to kings, ministers, and high officials, who should provide protection so that it does not decline or suffer loss;
they must uphold the torch of the True Dharma and turn the wheel of the True Dharma, ensuring it remains unceasing throughout the bounds of the future.

If one can practice in accordance with the teaching in this way, it will cause the dragon kings within the kingdom to rejoice; the winds will be harmonious and the rains timely, the various devas will be filled with joy, and there will be abundance, happiness, and peace. All calamities and misfortunes will be eliminated, the entire land will enjoy great tranquility, and the king’s person will be happy. He shall forever preserve his supreme position, his power of merit will be extended, and he will no longer have anxiety or distress. His lifespan will be increased, and his fame in the present life will pervade the ten directions.
The kings of foreign lands all praised him together, saying:
"The Son of Heaven of such-and-such a country is benevolent, humble, loyal, and filial; he transforms the people through the Dharma and relieves the common folk, being foremost among all kings."
"We shall now all take refuge and submit to this Great Dharma King; after casting off our bodies, we shall be born in the heavens to enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss, until we reach Bodhi!"
"Furthermore, Great King!
All phenomena are empty and void in their essential nature, impermanent, and subject to destruction.

It is like a person who, in a dream at night, sees a beautiful garden, mountains, rivers, and crowds of people, lush forests and clear springs, halls, houses, and towers—all of which are delightful; yet upon waking, not a single thing remains to be seen."

Great King, you should know that at the time of death, one must utterly abandon the royal throne one has inherited, as well as one’s lifespan, all forms of superior pleasure, sovereign nobility, and the delights of the five sensory desires; including elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; parents, brothers, sons, daughters, queens, and consorts; all the people of the nation down to ministers and attendants; gold, silver, precious jewels, clothing, food, drink, and all storehouses. Nothing remains.
All these various phenomena are dharmas subject to impermanence and destruction; they are difficult to preserve, their nature is unstable, and they ultimately end in dispersal.
They are objects of dread that give rise to suffering and affliction; they are devoid of self or what belongs to a self, and likewise lack any sovereign master.
"You should constantly practice observation and never be negligent.
Furthermore, Great King! It is like a great tree:
first leaves and flowers appear, then it bears fruit; once the fruit has ripened, it gradually falls away."
The green leaves turn yellow one after another, and subsequently all fall away until they are completely gone, leaving only the empty tree.
Once the tree has withered and dried, a great fire arrives; its fierce and blazing flames will, before long, consume it entirely.
"Furthermore, Great King!

It is like the sun and moon, which possess great power and are endowed with great radiance, able to cause all darkness to be completely dispelled; yet these too will, before long, ultimately meet with destruction."
"Great King!
You should thus contemplate the impermanence, selflessness, and the nature of disintegration and destruction, and give rise to fear and dread.
As a king, you should transform the realm through the Dharma; do not practice what is contrary to the Dharma. Constantly cultivate all manner of goodness and do not follow evil conduct."
"Furthermore, Great King!

It is like four great mountains, each from one of the four directions, coming together as a single, solid mass without any gaps. Reaching up to the vast sky above and grinding against the earth below, among all the grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and living beings therein, not a single creature—whether flying or running—could escape. There is no strong man who could resist them in combat, nor can they be turned back by means of incantations, medicines, or wealth."
"Great King!
The four mountains of the human world are likewise: namely, old age, sickness, death, and the loss of power.
Great King!"
When old age arrives, it causes one to wither and decline;
when illness strikes, it gives rise to suffering and affliction;
when the time of death manifests, one's life must inevitably be severed.
"If its momentum is lost at the opportune moment, its majestic power is extinguished.

Furthermore, Great King, it is like the lion king, swift and powerful, with claws and fangs so sharp that when he enters the midst of a herd of deer, he takes his food as he pleases without anyone able to obstruct him; these various beasts, intimidated by him, possess no autonomy."
"Great King, you should know that all sentient beings are struck by the arrow of death; they possess no strength or power, and have neither refuge nor protection.

When life is about to be severed, their joints and bones fall apart, their flesh and blood dry up, they are unable to speak, their hands and feet flail in confusion, and their vital energy is utterly exhausted."

Saliva and spittle, as well as excrement and urine, completely defile his body; the six sense organs, beginning with the eyes, are all obstructed; the breath is choked in the throat, and food and drink cannot pass.

In every moment of thought, the final consciousness is about to perish; from time immemorial, one has wandered through the ocean of suffering—birth, old age, sickness, and death—following the flow of karma.

At this very moment, as the life-faculty is about to be severed, the fruits of all past actions manifest before one; the messengers of Yama are most terrifying, and in the long night of darkness, there is no way to resist them.
The inhalation and exhalation of breath suddenly come to an end; one travels alone without a companion, filled with terror at every turn.
Leaving this human world and heading toward the next life, one is about to fall into a great pit and enter a place of deep darkness;
one must traverse a perilous path, yet possesses no further provisions for the journey.

"Blown by the winds of karma, they do not know the path ahead; at that time, when beset by calamity, there is no other refuge, and during this period, they must undergo retribution according to their karma. Great King!"
There is a dhāraṇī named "Victorious Banner.
If a person has previously received and upheld it, it will serve as a virtuous companion within the cycle of birth and death, providing mutual protection and rescue.
"Great King, listen well!
I shall now speak for you.
The mantra is as follows:"
“Namo Śākyamunaye tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya | Tadyathā | Oṃ śame śame sarvabādhā-praśamani svāhā. The Buddha said to the Great King: “This dhāraṇī was spoken by all the Buddhas.

If one daily cleanses oneself with water for rinsing the mouth and constantly recites it seven times, it possesses great majestic power capable of providing salvation—like encountering a blazing mass of fire when struck by extreme cold, or obtaining clear, cool water during a time of great heat.”
Seeking a path in the height of summer, one encounters the shade of a fine tree;
like one who is thirsty, one meets a clear spring;
like one who is hungry, one finds delicious food.
It is like a sick person who receives medicinal spells and further encounters a skilled physician;
it is like a timid and fearful person who finds a strong and courageous companion.
Great King!
When such a person of merit is about to die, auspicious signs appear to guide them.
Great King!
At that time, there is only wholesome dharma that mutually protects and attends to them, serving as their refuge; it is only this dhāraṇī that is truly capable of providing salvation.

Therefore, Great King, you should constantly recite this divine mantra day by day; it can eliminate all karmic obstacles and further cultivate immeasurable causes of merit. You should carefully observe that all things are impermanent, subject to decay, and ultimately empty and void. Conceive great terror toward the gateway of death, transform the world through goodness, refrain from practicing unwholesome dharmas, and constantly cultivate meritorious deeds while giving rise to great compassion.

Why is this? For this body is constantly cherished and protected; it is provided with the finest delicacies prepared by renowned chefs, and it rests at ease according to the season, free from anxiety and in a state of sovereignty.
"Although they enjoy such extraordinary pleasures, in the end they cannot avoid being oppressed by the fire of hunger at the moment of death, dying for lack of food.
Furthermore, Great King!"
The garments they wear are all exquisite—Kāśī silk, white cotton, brocade, damask, and gauze—providing comfort according to the season and their desires.

Yet, in the end, they cannot escape the moment of death: prostrate upon a bed, dependent on others for every turn, their bodies encrusted with filth and their robes drenched in secretions, causing those who behold them to feel revulsion.
"Furthermore, Great King!

During his lifetime, he bathed and adorned his body, anointing it with perfumes and powdered incense, embellishing himself with various ornaments, pervading himself with the fragrance of incense, and binding flower garlands upon his head."

Even if one were to enjoy such supreme and exquisite articles of pleasure, in the end they cannot avoid gradual transformation and decay; they return to their original form, and foulness manifests before one’s eyes, rendering bathing and the application of fragrant unguents entirely in vain.
"Furthermore, Great King!
Surrounded in the inner palace by many court ladies, with pipes and strings playing in succession and songs and dances performed at will, one passes the time in pleasure, hearing no news of sorrow;
yet in the end, one cannot avoid being pressed by the suffering of death, and one dies in a state of fear."
"Furthermore, Great King!
Your palace is adorned with various ornaments; its windows and doors are open and well-ventilated, and its temperature is perfectly regulated according to the seasons.
You may indulge your desires throughout the day and enjoy pleasures through the night."
In the chamber, bright lamps were lit; many court ladies were present, and fragrant incense wafted from latticed screens as famous flowers were strewn everywhere.
His bed was adorned with the seven precious gems, layered with fine rugs and cushions, and provided with pillows for reclining; he lay there at his ease, free from all further anxiety or toil.
When their karma is exhausted, they ultimately cannot escape death; after their bodies have perished, they are sent to the cold forest and placed in the empty wilderness.
Their corpses rot and disintegrate, with pus and blood flowing profusely;
their bones and flesh are scattered, and all people treat them with contempt and disdain.
It is devoured by foxes, wolves, owls, crows, eagles, and vultures.
Alas for this body!
It has ultimately come to this.

"Furthermore, Great King! On an auspicious morning and a festive occasion, you shall mount a solemn carriage and depart the city to visit the fragrant grove. There, you may indulge your heart in pleasure and appreciation, accompanied before and behind by elephants, horses, carriages, and foot-soldiers. Whatever vehicle you desire to ride, there shall be none that does not fulfill your wish. Your ministers and attendants shall maintain the decorum of ceremonial pheasant-feather fans, with canopies and curtains suspended high above, and golden parasols held aloft. As drums and music play in unison and bells and chimes resonate harmoniously, all people shall revere you as if you were Śakra, the Lord of Devas."
When one’s merit and lifespan are exhausted, the messengers of Yama arrive to seize the spirit and lead it before the King; there, judgment is rendered according to one’s deeds, and none can escape.

Only the remaining physical remains are left upon the ground, while parents, wives, children, and the people of the nation all wail together in grief, beating their breasts in anguish. The funeral bier carries the body to the charnel ground, where it is either cremated, buried, or cast into the water. When birds, beasts, fish, turtles, and crocodiles catch the scent of the flesh, they scramble to devour it until the bones turn to dust, no different from the earth itself.

"Great King, you should know that all sentient beings who possess consciousness are exactly like this: they are ultimately destroyed by impermanence; their essence is difficult to rely upon with confidence, as it shifts and changes from moment to moment; and this body of various afflictions is not something to be cherished."
"Who that possesses wisdom would not give rise to weary detachment? Therefore, Great King,
you should contemplate this body as the root of affliction, followed by impermanence, and constantly driven and oppressed by the King of Death."
Having understood this matter, you shall become a Dharma King; you must not indulge your passions by giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion, nor commit evil deeds. Why is this?
"Great King!

I do not say that there are foolish worldlings who, regarding the five objects of desire—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—constantly accumulate them in great measure and always delight in being close to them, yet such persons can give rise to wearying satisfaction."
"Great King!
Who is able to give rise to a mind of revulsion toward the objects of desire?

It is when noble ones (ārya) give rise to superior wisdom; only when this wisdom manifests before them does revulsion and contentment arise, whereby they gradually distance themselves from them and realize wondrous nirvāṇa."

At that time, the Devaputra Prabhāsa, having heard the Buddha’s teaching—that he would ensure his own well-being, long preserve his royal throne, benefit all sentient beings, have his fame spread throughout the ten directions, and eventually be reborn in heaven to enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss—[was filled with joy].

With deep hearts filled with joy and celebrating what they had never before experienced, they joined their palms in reverence, gazed up at the Buddha with single-minded devotion, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Out of great compassion, the Tathāgata has expounded for us such subtle and wondrous Dharma principles.”
"I now receive this upon my head and shall always vow to circulate it, so that all people throughout the nation may recite and study it.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Great King!
Having cultivated causes in previous lives, you now receive this superior retribution, becoming a son of heaven whose every wish is fulfilled according to his heart.
You should act as instructed and not be negligent!"
At that time, the Devaputra Prabhāsa and the great assembly were all filled with great joy; they accepted and practiced the teaching with faith, prostrated before the Buddha, and departed.
This concludes the *Rājadharmasūtra* spoken by the Buddha for the Devaputra Prabhāsa.
